title: When You're the Only Developer on the Project
summary: Building software alone is fast and free, but feedback goes missing and every decision lands on you. A few habits help: decision records, borrowed review, firm basics.
author: Nguyen Le Phong
html:
It's 11 p.m. The build is green, the feature works, and there's nobody around to tell. One tab has the product open, one has the logs, and a third has a half-written note explaining a decision nobody asked about. If you've ever shipped something on your own, you probably know the feeling: total freedom and total responsibility, sharing one desk.

This post is about that deal. Building alone has real upsides, and a few costs that creep in without you noticing. Most of those costs can be patched with small habits, and none of the habits need a team.

The good part is real

Solo work is fast. You don't book a meeting to move a button or wait for anyone to approve a refactor. The codebase stays consistent because one head holds all of it. For a while the speed feels amazing: you finally get to build without waiting on anybody.

Paul Graham explains why in Maker's Schedule, Manager's Schedule. People who make things tend to work in blocks of at least half a day, and "a single meeting can blow a whole afternoon." On your own, you get those long blocks by default. Enjoy them.

What goes missing

Then the other side shows up. Nobody catches the assumption you've been carrying for three days. Nobody says the signup flow is confusing, asks whether the feature is worth building at all, or wonders why the schema bends around one edge case.

You lose more than company. When Alberto Bacchelli and Christian Bird studied code review at Microsoft, they found that besides finding defects, reviews brought knowledge transfer, increased team awareness and alternative solutions to problems (Expectations, Outcomes, and Challenges of Modern Code Review). On a solo project all of those channels go silent at once. Feedback becomes optional, and optional feedback is the first thing you skip when you're tired.

The shape of the job changes too. Product scope, UX, database design, deploys, support, security, pricing, docs, bug triage: every decision comes back to the same person. When something breaks at night, the one who wrote it, runs it, explains it to users and fixes it is you. That builds strong ownership. It also eats your evenings bit by bit, unless you protect them.

Write it down for whoever joins next

That might be a future teammate, or you in six months, who is practically a stranger. Michael Nygard's architecture decision records fit solo work well: one short file per decision, kept in the repo, with the context, the decision, its status and its consequences. His point is that someone who finds an unexplained decision can only accept it blindly or reverse it blindly, and both are risky.

No ceremony needed. Five small files go a long way:

  • a decision log, one paragraph per decision
  • a setup note that gets a fresh laptop to a running app
  • a release checklist
  • a list of known risks
  • a rough architecture sketch

Together they work as a second memory outside your head, so tomorrow's work doesn't depend on how much energy you have left today. If you want more on that habit, there's a whole post on the note you return to later.

Borrow review from outside

Solo doesn't have to mean unreviewed. A friend can click through your main flow while you watch and resist the urge to explain. A community forum can answer a narrow technical question. A contractor can look over the payment or auth code, where one mistake costs real money. An AI assistant can flag missing tests or confusing names, as long as you check what it says before acting on it.

None of this replaces a team. It does break the echo chamber, and it gives you back some of what Bacchelli and Bird saw reviews doing: someone else learns your code, and you learn from their questions.

Split building time from running time

When any notification might be urgent, the day loses its shape. Teams get structure from process. Alone, you build it yourself, and it can stay small:

  • a few lines of planning every Monday
  • a fixed window for bug triage, so bugs don't eat every hour
  • a clear rule for what gets an answer right away (data loss, security, payments) and what waits for the window
  • a shutdown note at the end of the day: what you were in the middle of, and what comes next

It's Graham's maker schedule, applied to yourself. If support pings chop every afternoon into pieces too small for anything hard, you've rebuilt the meetings you left a team to avoid.

Pick the basics you won't skip

You can't build every guardrail a big company has, and you don't have to. A few things are worth holding firm on anyway: backups you've restored at least once, tests for the flows that touch money or user data, enough logging to see what broke, secrets kept out of the repo, dependencies kept current, and a written way to roll back. The point is to cover the spots where one small mistake would cost trust, money or a whole weekend.

You are not your product

This trap is easy to miss. When you build everything yourself, every bug starts to feel like a verdict on you. A user cancels, a week goes slowly, a screen looks awkward, and it all points back at one person.

Gerald Weinberg named the way out in 1971, in The Psychology of Computer Programming: egoless programming. Jeff Atwood's well-known summary, The Ten Commandments of Egoless Programming, puts the second one bluntly: "You are not your code." Software is a system working under constraints. A broken flow is a broken flow. Fix the flow and skip the self-punishment.

Try this week

  • Write one decision record for the last choice a stranger would question.
  • Ask someone outside the project to try your main flow for 15 minutes.
  • Set one triage window and a rule for what is allowed to interrupt it.
  • Restore one backup for real, to see that it works.
  • End Friday with a shutdown note, then close the laptop.

Can you carry the whole project alone? For a while, probably yes. The more useful question is which habit, document or person would make the work less lonely and help it last. Start with the smallest one.
